title: Proposed coffee tax 'already dead, buried' --Quimbo
summary: Any proposal that will impose a tax on coffee products is "dead for good," according to House ways and means panel chair Miro Quimbo of Marikina said.

blocks.text: Published November 27, 2026 12:35pm
Any proposal that will impose a tax on coffee products is "dead for good," according to House ways and means panel chair Miro Quimbo of Marikina said.
“Two days ago, dead on arrival po ‘yan. Pero ngayon po, hindi na po pinaglalamayan. Patay na po. Nailibing na po,” Quimbo said in an interview on Super Radyo DZBB
(It was dead on arrival two days ago. Now, there’s no wake. That’s dead and buried.)
Quimbo was responding to the proposal put forward by Olivia Limpe-Aw, Distilled Spirits Association of the Philippines (DSAP) president.
“Marami pong mapipinsala diyan, hindi lang iyong mga coffee farmers natin, pero pati iyong small coffee shops. Starbucks is not the only coffee shop,” Quimbo added.
(That would be devastating not just for coffee farmers, but also for small-time coffee shops.)
Quimbo said his committee is going after increased taxes on alcopops, which are flavored liquor laced with hard drinks such as rhum, margarita, and gin, but with an alcohol content of just 8%.
Tax rates on alcopops, Quimbo said, are way lower than beer due to alcohol content since it contains distilled spirits which are taxed higher.

Quimbo said alcopops should be taxed for what it is, a distilled spirit, and to discourage young people from drinking it because studies have shown that a person picking up a drinking habit early are likely to drink in their lifetime 35% of the time.
“While the alcohol content is just at 8%, those are hard drinks [in it]. That’s distilled sprits which are different from beer, and yet it is taxed lower than beer,” Quimbo said.
“We need to a separate category for alcopops for it to be taxed appropriately. Otherwise, people will just turn to alcopops and that would be more damaging to the health of our people,” Quimbo added.
Tax for airplanes, helicopters
Likewise, Quimbo said that taxes for the wealthy should come from the items they purchase, such as airplanes, helicopters, and luxury vehicles.
The wealth of the most wealthy, Quimbo said, could also come from dividends of the companies where they hold shares, and the value of such shares could also increase over time.
“We are targeting their consumption pattern. Di kayo siguro maniniwala, pero wala pong excise tax ang helicopter, speedboat, jetski. Papatawan po natin ng excise tax po ‘yan,” Quimbo said.
“Some would say that [kind of tax] will only give us a small amount to collect. But that collection still counts,” Quimbo added.
Quimbo said that as it is. taxes for luxury vehicles are just at 50% of the landed cost or the selling price of the dealer, provided that the cost is over P4 million.

“We are proposing to peg the tax at 75% of the actual selling price, and that includes those motorcycles which engines are high powered. If you have a motorcycle at 1000 cc [which cost over P665,000 a unit], sigurado tayo na ang gumagamit nito ay talagang mayayaman,” Quimbo said.
“Again, we need to target the wealth tax at their consumption behavior,” he added. —Llanesca Panti/ VAL, GMA News
